text:
R282 — T1 CPU pool worker/task experiment admission and matched recipe
Date: 2026-10-12
Status: read-only source/report audit. No source changes, builds, tests, GPU work, profilers, process/service operations, Git operations, or cleanup.

## Finding

The reported T1 callback span is a reasonable reason to consider a bounded worker-scaling experiment, but it does not establish that more workers will shorten decode. The closed 32K + GEN16 receipt reports 16 windows at T=1 and 124.09 ms/window: GPU-reach wait 50.27 ms, per-layer host 55.16 ms including CPU callback 50.64 ms, stage 0.49 ms, and commit/emit 2.65 ms. The 50.64 ms is callback wall time, not summed CPU-core time. The same receipt is explicitly `performance_sample_eligible=false`, has `validation_and_tracing_overhead=true`, and is from an earlier WN/binary than the parent-specified 338fe source. Use it to motivate and shape the trial; do not use its throughput or CPU/GPU relation as the A/B performance baseline for 338fe.

On the parent-specified source, both CLI settings are real and independently reach the serving decode pool. For a clean first worker comparison, hold row-task count at 18 across workers 3, 4, and 5. This makes 5 workers / 18 tasks equivalent to the existing auto default on the six-physical-core host, while avoiding the confound that auto changes from 12 to 15 to 18 tasks as worker count rises. Only after the worker sweep should a small independent task sweep compare 6, 12, 18, and 24 at the selected worker count. These settings change task partition and claim count, not the algorithm or expert routing.

This remains a test proposal. It cannot predict which arm wins or whether the remaining callback time is row-kernel work, DRAM/cache service, atomic claim/barrier overhead, or a combination.

## The existing measurement and its limits

The closed receipt is `/home/yayoi/.local/state/strata-sycl/post-reboot-tuning-20261007/main-decode-criticalpath-model-root-v1/xe-timed1-on/record.json`, SHA-256 `de826d6cd915b121801ebb3ba5d5f86f0945d82ae6f0819a59bc974c094b71dc`. It is inactive, passed/complete, but not a performance-eligible sample; its own `validation_and_tracing_overhead` field is true. Its source executable is from `sync-xe-v0143-nonfinite-20261012`, not the R282 source worktree, so the proposed source-version experiment must use one identical target-source binary for all worker/task arms.

The recorded exact input token IDs are 32,768 tokens from `tokens.txt`, SHA-256 `94cbdd7fdc6c9f32a08c0c4f8b50c1cc27a7ffc3f383d23c5c6ac24e8ec7f2c9`; the receipt records 16 generated tokens, normal length completion, and output IDs:
`40, 3172, 22903, 411, 42903, 4560, 1970, 57710, 11, 20434, 383, 55404, 21851, 11, 5438, 7465`.
The SHA-256 of their newline-delimited decimal IDs (final newline included) is `541fd69271b343b49151becce750ded3ae51bc34f583700806fd71c7f44b7d31`.

This run used 262,144 max context, int8 KV with 32,768 resident, 128 expert-cache option plus per-layer mode (effective INFO reports 144 slots / 281 MiB), PCIe fraction zero, greedy decode, `--spec 4` with `mtp_max=0`, `--no-spec-split`, prefill chunk 8192 and 16 prefill experts, and no prefill borrow. It observed 9.45 CPU expert entries and 0.55 VRAM hits per layer-window, PCIe zero. Keep the exact request, model/pack/profile, flags, environment, topology, and prompt input fixed in future arms; mutate only pool workers/tasks. The recorded `INFO` proves pool workers 5, but it does not report effective per-thread CPU IDs.

The same request's GPU-reach wait and CPU callback numbers are not exclusive CPU/GPU work measurements. The verifier has segmented device/host handoff, while `expert_pool_dispatch_multi` publishes the GPU plan before CPU work and can run the selected GPU share beside CPU misses. Keep the existing route and handoff behavior identical; do not treat the two measured spans as independent additive compute requirements or use a “CPU-only” inference assumption.

## Why the knobs apply to serving T=1

On the audited source path, `serve/server.py:2125–2145` starts with the config's `args` unchanged and appends server-derived settings; the engine config is therefore the route for both pool CLI options. `generate.cpp:2273–2284` parses `--pool-workers` and strict `--pool-tasks` values (0 through `ExpertPool::kMaxTasks`, 4096). At startup, `generate.cpp:4079–4084` passes them directly to `ExpertPool` and prints effective task/participating-thread counts. There is no pool-workers or pool-tasks environment-variable alias in the searched engine source. `STRATA_POOL_SPIN_US` is a separate test knob for idle spin-before-sleep; it is not a worker/task count control and must remain unchanged.

The exact T=1 path is not the old single-expert `run()` path. `expert_pool_dispatch_multi` accepts `n_tok=1`, forms the `n_tok*k` route-entry plan, groups duplicate CPU misses by expert ID, and appends one `ExpertJobMulti` per distinct CPU expert; each such job has `nt=1` in this window. For a native layer with at least one CPU job, it unconditionally calls `run_split_multi_native` (`expert_source.cpp:1755–1776, 1938–1980, 1983–1991`). This is the actual caller reached by T=1. Cache hits, GPU-offloaded rows, duplicates, and invalid IDs do not create CPU jobs; zero CPU jobs skip the pool call.

`run_split_multi_native` executes GU rows, then caller-thread intermediate quantization, then Down rows. Per phase `phase_tasks(rows)` returns either `3*(workers + host_participant)` for automatic 0, or `min(rows, explicit_tasks)` (`pool.cpp:409–410, 470–505`). With one CPU expert, the work dimensions are FF=640 GU rows and H=2560 Down rows on the supplied model; with n distinct CPU experts they are `n*640` and `n*2560`. Thus 6/12/18/24 tasks are all representable whenever at least one expert is on CPU; each is below both row totals. If `n=0`, there is no phase/task experiment for that layer. More tasks split the same flattened ranges into smaller equal row slices and increase task claims; they do not add weight bytes or move intermediate activation quantization into the pool.

Task assignment is dynamic, not expert-to-core ownership. `pool.cpp:301–379` claims task indices from the shared epoch/head and executes equal contiguous row ranges across the flattened experts. Each worker has private scratch. The host participates in the same claim loop by default. `run_phase` waits for workers to park, publishes a phase, lets host drain, waits for all tasks, and waits for workers to re-park (`pool.cpp:381–390`). Increasing tasks may reduce a tail if task costs vary; it also increases shared counter claims and slices one expert's contiguous rows among more workers. In a T=1 layer each expert's row calls share that layer's format and each job has one token, which reduces within-layer job-cost variation relative to a mix of formats. There is no per-worker CPU-time or wait-state telemetry in the ordinary decode timing receipt, so neither explanation can be selected from this source alone.

## Worker/core placement and actual logging

`physical_cores()` walks the inherited allowed CPU set and uses Linux package/core sysfs identity to select one logical CPU per physical core. `physical_cores(true)` drops its first selected core; the session-owned `SessionLoopScratch::init` pins the serving caller to the first core from `physical_cores(false)` (`pool.cpp:20–65, session.cpp:539–567`). The pool then pins worker i to selected core i for `i < available worker cores`; with the six-core supplied topology, workers 3/4/5 are all pinned to the first 3/4/5 cores after the host core (`pool.cpp:133–157`). Default host participation means total participants are 4/5/6 for explicit worker counts 3/4/5. `--no-host-worker` disables host job execution but is not part of this sweep: it changes participant count and automatic task count and tests a separate question.

The runner should keep its allowed-CPU mask and CPU/core topology fixed and record them with each arm. Source startup logging prints `CPU pool tasks/phase` and participant count, and the server `INFO` includes pool worker count; it does not log each thread's selected CPU ID. The source mapping is deterministic for a fixed inherited mask, but the log alone is not proof of the machine's effective mask or of where the OS actually ran threads.

## Smallest useful matched experiment after authorization

First close the current Main-owned run and confirm the target source/build and 32K/GEN16 comparison are admitted. Do not inspect or modify a live Main record. Build or use one frozen binary from the specified 338fe source only when the owner authorizes measurement; use that identical binary for all arms. The old R272 binary is not an arm.

The baseline request's args are in the closed receipt. Preserve the complete argv/environment and request protocol, including pack/native model, 262144 max context, KV/cache/profile, `--pcie-frac 0`, adaptive swaps 0, cache/per-layer mode, greedy, spec4 with effective `mtp_max=0`, no spec split, prefill options, and no other concurrent workload. Reuse the exact 32,768 token-ID prompt file by ID (do not re-tokenize), one request, and exactly 16 generated tokens. For task control, set explicit `--pool-tasks 18`; this is equivalent to the existing workers=5 automatic default on the recorded six-core host. Keep everything else unchanged.

Run one-at-a-time fresh-engine arms, with order interleaved across repeats:

- worker scaling: `(pool-workers, pool-tasks) = (3,18), (4,18), (5,18)`;
- if callback CPU remains material and the worker sweep is consistent, task scaling at the best worker count: task counts `6,12,18,24`.

The existing default `(5,0)` is auto=18 on this 6-core topology. A fresh `(5,18)` anchor confirms the explicit knob maps to the same partition count before interpreting the worker arms. For strict smallest screening, make the first three worker arms at least two fresh processes each; retain individual samples and every failed/invalid process. Repeat only if the paired distribution is ambiguous, not to chase a best run. If task count 18 is not reported at startup or startup `INFO`/effective settings differ, reject the arm as mismatched.

Before any clean performance sample, use at most one controlled diagnostic request per configuration (or equivalent existing validated route evidence) with `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` to confirm 16 windows, average T=1, CPU-job/cache/PCIe route, and effective worker/task counts. Keep `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE` and any profiler off. Because the R272 record marked tracing overhead and performance ineligible, keep these diagnostics out of the clean performance distribution. For clean arms, unset that diagnostic flag and use the controller's exact protocol wall boundaries from `REUSED` to `DONE` as decode wall, plus full-request/TTFT as a separate result; do not use full GEN wall as a decode metric. Pool’s `pool multi`/`ms_multi_*` summary accumulates pool-lifetime phase spans and can include prefill CPU-share work, so do not treat it as request-local unless the owner captures request deltas. The outer decode timing line is request-local but instrumented.

Correctness and route fingerprints for every arm: pass/complete, normal exit, exact 32,768 prompt IDs/hash, 16 generated output IDs and output-ID SHA identical to the baseline, finish=length, effective INFO (context/KV/cache/spec/worker count), startup `CPU pool tasks/phase`, no error/nonfinite/fault, actual one-token window count/shape from a separate diagnostic, identical CPU entries/cache hits/PCIe zero in that diagnostic, and unchanged output/logprob validation under the existing qualification. If output IDs differ, preserve the failure and stop the performance comparison pending numerical investigation. Do not enable `STRATA_STATE_HASH` for the timed arm: it adds device sync and changes the measured path.

Do not run workers or task arms concurrently with each other, another model request, or an active Main-owned GPU workload. This experiment needs the model's normal GPU execution; the exclusion is other concurrent work that would contend for the GPU/CPU/memory, not a claim that CPU and GPU work inside the inference are non-overlapping. Do not use `--no-pool`, `--gpu-only-full`, `--graph-only`, profile timings, or change PCIe/cache/prefill/speculative controls to create a false CPU floor.

## Interpretation gates: worker capacity, bandwidth, reductions, and scheduler cost

The row-pool phases perform GU and Down separately; intermediate H/FF quantization is serial on the caller. `CPU 50.64` surrounds the whole native expert dispatch execution (`d.ms_run`, set from after planning/ActQ/job formation through pool execution/remote finish), not just worker row code. In the timing line the pool callback is nested inside per-layer host time. Consequently worker-count gains can be limited by serial planning/activation quantization or route/copy handoff even if CPU workers get faster. Keep planning/route counters, stage and GPU-reach spans, decode wall, and request completion paired; do not add nested spans as an Amdahl decomposition.

The 32K receipt has roughly 9.45 CPU experts/layer-window and zero PCIe entries, enough to suggest that CPU jobs are usually present in this T=1 path, but these are averages for the diagnostic request and not per-layer stable counts for future arms. R213's 80.5–84.6 microsecond NT1 Down20 calibration is a host-resident actual-weight/synthetic-activation component measurement, not a production-call latency or physical memory-bandwidth measurement; its pool fit/holdout gates failed. R231 found existing pool-vs-direct speed differences in its native fixture, but the comparison changes participants and does not measure per-worker CPU time or memory-controller bytes. Neither report supplies a RAM ceiling for this decode request.

The pool source notes an older five-worker 33.7 GB/s result versus a measured one-thread 44.14 GB/s benchmark scaled to 36.8 GB/s for five of six cores (`pool.cpp` historical comment around 528–533). Treat that as a source comment about a prior test, not a current T1 bandwidth result. It motivates worker counts 3–5, but does not identify saturation or memory stalls on the present request. If 3→4→5 reduces CPU callback and decode wall while route/output remain fixed, report only a measured setting effect. If it plateaus, do not call it DRAM saturation without counters. If workers change `CPU` but not `REUSED`→`DONE`, GPU/serial stages or overlap may be the exposed wall limit. A task sweep can show whether a different partition count changes results at fixed workers; it cannot by itself prove atomic contention or worker imbalance. If the task sweep is flat or noisy, stop rather than add workers/tasks/profiling axes.

## Other-engine contrast (primary sources)

llama.cpp's CPU backend exposes a shared atomic `current_chunk` for work distribution in its threadpool, with per-thread state, and its model graph routes MoE layers through `build_moe_ffn` (`ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c`, `src/models/llama.cpp`). This is a concrete contrast in placement: Strata's native path aggregates host misses into per-expert jobs, flattens each layer's GU/Down rows into equal ranges, and dynamically claims task ranges from its epoch/head counter; llama.cpp builds MoE graph operations and relies on backend CPU operator parallelism. Do not compare throughput across engines as a worker-count prediction.

AMD's llama.cpp ZenDNN backend documentation explicitly lists `MUL_MAT_ID` (expert-based matrix multiplication) as supported for the ZenDNN LowOHA MatMul path and says unsupported types fall back to standard CPU; it also cautions that token-generation gains vary with model, batch size, threads, and topology. This illustrates a different way to accelerate CPU MoE at the operator/backend level, but its published support is Q8_0/FP32/BF16 and does not establish support for Strata's native IQ formats or the Ryzen 5 5600X's current kernel path. Sources: [ggml CPU threadpool source](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c), [llama.cpp model MoE graph construction](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/src/models/llama.cpp), [llama.cpp ZenDNN backend documentation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/backend/ZenDNN.md). The ZenDNN documentation is primary project documentation; the llama.cpp RFC for expert-cache is a discussion/proposal, not an adopted implementation and is not used to claim measured results.
